replace: statement

Methamphetamine's plasma elimination half-life is about 11 hours after smoked, intranasal or intravenous use, a figure cited second-hand in a narrative review (Kish, 2008); the primary pharmacokinetic studies, and the data on onset and bioavailability by route, have not yet been read.

In controlled-administration studies in adults, methamphetamine's plasma elimination half-life is about 10 to 12 hours and varies little by route: 10.7 hours (SD 2.4) after an intranasal and 10.7 hours (SD 2.1) after a smoked dose, with 11.0 to 11.8 hours for an intravenous reference dose given in the same sessions to the same 8 men (Harris et al., 2003); geometric means of 11.1 hours (smoked) and 12.2 hours (intravenous) in 6 men, with individual values from 8.3 to 18.2 hours (Cook et al., 1993); and 9.3 hours (SD 3.7) and 11.1 hours (SD 7.2) after single 10 mg and 20 mg sustained-release oral doses (Schepers et al., 2003). The figure applies to d-methamphetamine, the isomer given in those three studies: in a double-blind crossover, intravenous l-methamphetamine had a half-life of 13.3 to 15.0 hours against 10.2 to 10.7 hours for d-methamphetamine (Mendelson et al., 2006). Time to peak plasma concentration is a separate quantity that depends on route and formulation, and the active metabolite amphetamine has a longer half-life (about 15 to 17 hours) than the parent drug. Every study is small (6 to 12 participants), none randomized the order of routes except the enantiomer crossover, and the participants' own patterns of use were light or not reported.

set.plain: Meth leaves the blood slowly: after the level in the blood peaks, it takes about 10 to 12 hours to fall by half, and this is much the same whether it was snorted, smoked, injected or swallowed. People differ (about 8 to 18 hours in one study). The mirror-image form of the molecule, l-methamphetamine, stays longer. How long the drug can be measured in blood is not the same as how long its effects last.
set.magnitude: t½ about 10–12 h: intranasal 10.7 h (SD 2.39) and smoked 10.7 h (SD 2.11), with the intravenous reference 11.8 h (SD 3.59) and 11.0 h (SD 2.68) in the same men (n=8; Harris et al., 2003); smoked 11.1 h and intravenous 12.2 h as geometric means, individual range 8.3–18.2 h (n=6; Cook et al., 1993); oral sustained-release 9.3 h (SD 3.7) and 11.1 h (SD 7.2) (n=7 and n=5; Schepers et al., 2003). By enantiomer, intravenous: d 10.2–10.7 h against l 13.3–15.0 h (P<.0001; n=12; Mendelson et al., 2006). Clearance about 0.19–0.27 L·h⁻¹·kg⁻¹ and volume of distribution about 3.2–4.3 L/kg across these studies; the metabolite amphetamine 15.2–16.9 h.
set.population: Adults given single doses of methamphetamine in controlled-administration studies (6 to 12 participants per study; intranasal, smoked, intravenous or oral sustained-release)
set.exposure: Single methamphetamine dose (study conditions: 50 mg intranasal and 40 mg placed in the device for the smoked condition with a 10 mg intravenous reference; about 30 mg placed in the device with a 15.4–15.5 mg intravenous dose; 10 or 20 mg oral sustained-release; 0.25 and 0.5 mg/kg intravenous in the enantiomer study)
set.outcome: Plasma elimination half-life (with clearance, volume of distribution and the metabolite's half-life)
set.grade.domains.risk_of_bias.note: Small unblinded studies without randomized route order, except the Latin-square crossover of Mendelson et al. (2006).
set.grade.reasoning: Controlled-administration studies with a within-person intravenous reference start high (METHODS §6.3). Risk of bias −1: three of the four studies were unblinded and did not randomize the order of conditions, two had no placebo, and the samples are 6 to 12 people (card judgments: high for Harris et al., Cook et al. and Schepers et al.; some concerns for Mendelson et al.). Indirectness is no longer downgraded: the parameter is now measured directly in four primary studies rather than taken from a narrative review that cited another review. Inconsistency 0: four studies in three independent laboratories (Research Triangle Institute with North Carolina, the NIDA intramural programme, and San Francisco) agree within about two hours across four routes. Imprecision 0 for the central estimate, while the statement carries the individual range of about 8 to 18 hours. The enantiomer difference rests on a single study and is reported as such. The second-hand anchor to Kish (2008) is kept only as the trail from the earlier draft and may be dropped by the editor.

evidence_add.locator: Tables I and II, continuation columns (t1/2, CL, Vss)
evidence_add.extracted: Terminal half-life in the same 8 men: 10.7 h (SD 2.39) after the intranasal and 10.7 h (SD 2.11) after the smoked condition, with 11.8 h (SD 3.59) and 11.0 h (SD 2.68) for the intravenous reference dose given in the same sessions; clearance 272 and 271 mL·h⁻¹·kg⁻¹ and steady-state volume of distribution 4.30 and 4.02 L/kg.

evidence_add.locator: Results › Concentrations in Body Fluids and Pharmacokinetic Analysis (p. 718, continuing on p. 719); Table 1, Half-life and Total clearance rows with footnotes b and c (p. 719)
evidence_add.extracted: In 6 men given both routes, the geometric mean plasma half-life was 11.1 h after the smoked and 12.2 h after the intravenous condition (arithmetic means 11.8 h, SE 1.35, and 13.1 h, SE 1.54), with individual values from 8.3 to 18.2 h; total clearance after the intravenous dose was 0.192 L·h⁻¹·kg⁻¹ (SE 0.0097) and the volume of distribution in the elimination phase 3.24 and 3.73 L/kg.

After a single oral dose of a sustained-release formulation, the plasma half-life was 9.3 h (SD 3.7) at 10 mg and 11.1 h (SD 7.2) at 20 mg, with peak concentrations of 20.2 and 32.4 µg/L reached at 5.4 h (SD 2.5) and 7.5 h (SD 3.4).

evidence_add.locator: Table I, t½ and CL rows (all six dosing conditions)
evidence_add.extracted: In the double-blind crossover, the half-life of intravenous d-methamphetamine was 10.2 h (SD 2.3), 10.3 h (SD 2.6) and 10.7 h (SD 2.6) in the three conditions containing it, against 13.6 h (SD 3.8), 13.3 h (SD 3.5) and 15.0 h (SD 4.6) for l-methamphetamine; clearance 0.257 to 0.266 against 0.188 to 0.221 L·h⁻¹·kg⁻¹, with the same volume of distribution.

evidence_add.locator: Tables III and IV, continuation columns (t1/2 and the amphetamine/methamphetamine AUC ratio)
evidence_add.extracted: The active metabolite outlasts the parent drug: amphetamine's terminal half-life was 15.2 to 16.9 h across the four conditions, and its AUC was 15.5 to 19.3% of that of methamphetamine.

evidence_add.locator: Discussion, paragraph beginning 'The regression analysis did not indicate dose to be a significant variable'
evidence_add.extracted: Pooling the oral, smoked and intravenous data, the mean elimination rate constant fell as the absorbed dose rose (r² = 0.7042, P = 0.037), which the authors read as possible dose-dependent kinetics with a saturable renal process; the half-life quoted here therefore belongs to the low dose range studied.

change: Primary pharmacokinetic studies read in full (Harris et al., 2003; Cook et al., 1993; Schepers et al., 2003; Mendelson et al., 2006) replace the second-hand figure taken from a narrative review: half-life about 10–12 h by four routes, with the individual range, clearance, volume of distribution, the metabolite's longer half-life and the enantiomer difference. Statement, plain text, magnitude, population, exposure and outcome rewritten; certainty low → moderate (indirectness downgrade removed, risk of bias kept at one level); status single-study → replicated (three independent laboratories); verification draft → metadata-verified, because the claim no longer rests only on a narrative review (METHODS §6.3, §12) — the editor should confirm this rung. Six anchors added (ai-located, AI reader 6). The Kish (2008) anchor is now superseded and may be dropped.

evidence_add.extracted: In 8 men, the intranasal condition gave a peak plasma concentration of 113 ng/mL (SD 23.1) at 2.66 h (SD 1.16) and the smoked condition 50.9 ng/mL (SD 24.7) at 2.47 h (SD 3.91); plasma was sampled for three days, so the intranasal plasma peak is reached at about 2 to 3 hours and not later. This laboratory is independent of the two studies the claim rests on, but the design differed: no placebo, and an intravenous dose was infused in the same session.

change: Harris et al. (2003), read in full, bounds the open question in the statement: with plasma sampled to 72 hours, the intranasal peak came at 2.66 h (SD 1.16), so the true peak is at about 2–3 hours and not later than the 3–4-hour samples of the two studies the claim rests on. Anchor added (ai-located, AI reader 6); the caveat about the peak possibly being later is qualified rather than removed, because the two anchored studies sampled no further.

evidence_add.locator: Results, last paragraph of p. 1208 continuing into the 1st paragraph of p. 1209; Figure 4 (p. 1210)
evidence_add.extracted: 11 men who had used only methamphetamine (other illicit drug use excluded by SCID) against 9 men who had not: dopamine transporter binding potential (k3/k4, [11C]WIN-35,428) 3.51 (SD 0.45) against 4.40 (SD 0.18) in the caudate/putamen, 20.2% lower, and 2.93 (SD 0.77) against 4.16 (SD 0.64) in the nucleus accumbens, 29.6% lower; Mann-Whitney U = 1.0 and 8.5, N = 20, both p<0.001.

replace: statement

Three cross-sectional analyses, including this programme's own baseline study, found no relation between time since last use and transporter levels (Volkow et al., 2001a; Johanson et al., 2006, and McCann et al., 2008, as described by Hart et al., 2012).

Four cross-sectional analyses, including this programme's own baseline study, found no relation between time since last use and transporter levels (Volkow et al., 2001a; Sekine et al., 2001, read in full, in 11 men abstinent from 7 days to 1.5 years; Johanson et al., 2006, and McCann et al., 2008, as described by Hart et al., 2012); all are small, so they bound recovery rather than exclude it.

evidence_add.locator: Table 1, Duration of Abstinence column (p. 1207); Results, 2nd paragraph (p. 1209); Figure 5 (p. 1211)
evidence_add.extracted: In 11 men abstinent from 7 days to 1.5 years, dopamine transporter binding potential did not correlate with the duration of abstinence in either the caudate/putamen or the nucleus accumbens, while in the same 11 men it did correlate with the duration of use (Kendall's tau −0.48 and −0.73). A non-significant rank correlation in 11 people is weak evidence either way, and the authors nonetheless read it as showing that the reduction is long-lasting.

change: A fourth cross-sectional null added from a primary source read in full (Sekine et al., 2001: no correlation between transporter binding and abstinence of 7 days to 1.5 years in 11 men), with the statement noting that these small studies bound recovery rather than exclude it, and that the same study's authors read their null as evidence of persistence. Anchor added (ai-located, AI reader 6).

evidence_add.locator: Discussion, paragraph beginning 'In a previous study using the same PET scanner'
evidence_add.extracted: Measured with the same scanner and tracer by the same group, unmedicated Parkinson's disease showed a striatal dopamine transporter reduction of about 80%, against roughly 20% in the methamphetamine group here, none of whom had parkinsonism or other neurological abnormality; the authors argue that in people who use methamphetamine a small reduction predicts psychiatric rather than motor signs.

change: Primary anchor added for the sentence that the pattern differs from Parkinson's disease: Sekine et al. (2001), read in full, compared about 20% striatal transporter reduction in their methamphetamine group with about 80% in unmedicated Parkinson's disease measured with the same scanner and tracer, in people with no parkinsonian signs. No wording changed (ai-located, AI reader 6).

replace: statement

The two amounts were given to different, very small groups whose assignment is not described as randomized, and they were not compared statistically, so the difference may reflect the people as much as the money.

The two amounts were given to different, very small groups whose assignment is not described as randomized, and they were not compared statistically, so the difference may reflect the people as much as the money. In an earlier 20-day residential study from the same laboratory group, 8 volunteers with stimulant experience (only 3 of whom reported ever having used methamphetamine) chose an oral capsule over a $1 voucher on a mean of 4.3 of 8 occasions when it contained 5 mg of methamphetamine and 4.4 when it contained 10 mg, against 1.4 and 1.3 in the matched placebo conditions (P<0.02 and P<0.01), with no difference between the two doses; that comparison was double-blind and within person, but the two studies share investigators and setting, so they are not independent replications (Hart et al., 2001).
plain

Different men got different amounts and the groups were tiny, so the study cannot show that more money caused the difference. In an earlier study from the same lab, eight volunteers who lived in a laboratory for 20 days chose a capsule over a $1 voucher about four times out of eight when it contained meth, and about once when it was a dummy capsule.

Imprecision: 7 and 6 participants, no test statistics. The drug-versus-placebo comparison now added from Hart et al. (2001) is of a different kind: double-blind, within person, with counterbalanced dose order, which under METHODS §6.3 starts high. The displayed certainty is unchanged because it is set by the money comparison; the senior author may wish to split the claim so that 'an oral or intranasal methamphetamine dose is chosen over placebo' and 'a larger monetary alternative reduces drug choice' are rated separately.

set.population: Adults with stimulant experience, not seeking treatment, in laboratory choice studies (13 men in the intranasal study; 8 residential volunteers, 1 of them a woman, in the oral study)
set.exposure: Opportunity to self-administer portions of a methamphetamine or d-amphetamine dose, or an oral methamphetamine capsule (study conditions: 5 and 10 mg)
set.comparator: An alternative of money: $5 (7 participants) or $20 (6 participants) sampled and chosen in 10% portions in one study; a $1 voucher per choice occasion in the other; placebo capsules in the matched conditions
set.magnitude: Drug choices 41% ($5) vs 17% ($20) overall (Abstract); about 47–50% at the 50 mg/70 kg condition with $5 (Discussion). Oral study: mean 4.3 of 8 choices at 5 mg and 4.4 at 10 mg against 1.4 and 1.3 in the matched placebo conditions (P<0.02 and P<0.01), with vouchers chosen on about 80% of occasions under placebo.

evidence_add.locator: Results › Reinforcing effects (p. 77, right column, continuing on p. 78); Figure 1 (p. 78)
evidence_add.extracted: In a residential study, 8 volunteers chose a capsule over a $1 voucher on a mean of 4.3 of 8 occasions when it contained 5 mg of methamphetamine and 4.4 when it contained 10 mg, against 1.4 and 1.3 in the matched placebo conditions (P<0.02 and P<0.01); the two active doses did not differ from each other, nor the two placebo conditions.

Of the 8 completers (1 woman, 7 men, aged 23 to 42, mean 31.1), only 3 reported ever having used methamphetamine while 7 reported having used cocaine at least once; of the 11 who began, 3 did not complete, one of them because of difficulty sleeping during the 10 mg phase.

evidence_add.locator: Discussion, paragraph beginning 'There are at least two possible explanations'
evidence_add.extracted: The authors' evidence that the $1 voucher was a working alternative is that vouchers were chosen on about half of the occasions when methamphetamine was available and on about 80% of occasions under placebo; they also note that the dose range tested may have been too narrow for a dose effect to appear.

change: Hart et al. (2001) read in full and added: a double-blind residential choice study in which an oral methamphetamine capsule was chosen over a $1 voucher about four times in eight against about one in eight for placebo, with no difference between 5 mg and 10 mg. Statement, plain text, population, exposure, comparator and magnitude widened to cover both studies; status single-study → replicated by the same team (both from the same laboratory group). Three anchors added (ai-located, AI reader 6). The GRADE reasoning now records that the drug-versus-placebo part of the claim rests on a within-person double-blind comparison that would start high, and asks the senior author whether the claim should be split.
